changes.before: Change ratio to Box<int> but keep {1.5}. What happens?
changes.after: Use a class template to store a chosen type of value.

before: template<typename T> can parameterize a class. Box<int> and Box<double> are distinct types. Each stores a T and exposes a copy through get().

Box(T value) : item{value} initializes the member using the constructor input. explicit keeps construction deliberate. We spell the template argument at the call site rather than introducing class-template deduction here.

Expected output or behavior: 3 1.5
. Local compiler test evidence is recorded separately from app reading completion.
Optional local transfer task: Instantiate Box<std::string> after including <string>, then retrieve its value. You may trace this without a compiler; finishing the reading is not proof of a local run.
after: A class template is a pattern for classes with different types. T is its type placeholder. Box<int> stores an int, while Box<double> stores a double. They are two distinct types made from the same pattern.
The constructor receives a T value and uses item{value} to initialize its member. get() returns a copy of that member. explicit keeps construction from silently converting an input into a Box.
The program prints 3 1.5. count is a Box<int> holding three. ratio is a Box<double> holding one and a half.
Choosing Box<int> fixes its stored type as int. Braces reject a starting value that would need a narrowing conversion, meaning a conversion that could lose information.

after.question: Change ratio to Box<int> but keep the initializer {1.5}. What happens?
choices: The value silently rounds to two.
The compiler rejects the conversion that would lose the fractional part.
Both boxes change their type to double.
after.explanation: The chosen Box<int> needs an int input. Brace initialization rejects the fractional double value.
